quiz.title: Chapter 12 Quiz: Ethics and Professional Responsibility
quiz.intro: Ten questions on the rules behind the research, the consequences of getting it wrong, and the method steps that keep you safe.

items.q: Model Rule 1.1 requires competent representation, which includes:
options: The legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation, including keeping abreast of relevant technology
items.why: Comment 8 speaks directly to technology (The Duty of Competence).

items.q: The ST Engineering Marine decision is used to show:
options: The core competence failure: relying on older authority without checking whether the law had moved
That malpractice never follows research errors
items.why: The closing-out protocol’s citator update is designed to prevent exactly this (The Duty of Competence).

items.q: Rule 3.3 creates an affirmative research obligation because it:
options: Requires you to cite every case
Requires disclosure of directly adverse controlling authority the other side has not cited, so you must search for adverse authority
items.why: Hence the adverse-authority search in the closing-out protocol (The Duty of Candor).

items.q: Rules 5.1 and 5.3 make the Research Log matter because:
options: The log is filed with the court
Supervisors must review delegated research, and the log is the reviewable record of what was searched, found, and why the research was judged complete
items.why: If your supervisor questions your work, the log gives a complete, defensible record (The Duty to Supervise).

items.q: Shields v. Town of Perrysville illustrates which consequence?
options: Waiver: contentions with no citation to legal authority are waived
items.why: Inadequate research can forfeit an argument entirely (Consequences of Inadequate Legal Research).

items.q: In re Martin (Bankr. N.D. Ill. 2025) says:
options: Lawyers may not use generative AI
No lawyer should use a generative AI product to perform research without verifying the results
Verification is optional for experienced lawyers
items.why: The duty of competence requires verification of all research, whatever its source (AI and Emerging Technology Considerations).

items.q: A fabricated citation that came from a chatbot is:
options: Excused because the lawyer did not write it
A Rule 3.3 problem exactly as if it came from anywhere else
A problem only if opposing counsel notices
items.why: Whether you found it through Westlaw or a chatbot is irrelevant (Common Pitfalls).

options: Running every case through a citator and checking every statute’s current text before finalizing a document
Asking the AI to verify its own citations
Checking only the cases you quote
items.why: These are the closing steps of the Question Method, performed with the rules in view (Build Verification Into Your Research Workflow).

items.q: Which method step does the chapter pair with Rule 3.3?
options: The adverse-authority search in the closing-out protocol’s final sweep
items.why: Rule 1.1 pairs with the citator update and read-before-you-cite check; Rules 5.1 and 5.3 with the Research Log (The chapter in one glance).

items.q: Royal Oak Entertainment v. City of Royal Oak shows courts may respond to inadequate research with:
options: Fee awards: counsel and client held liable for the fees the other side incurred because of the research failure
items.why: Sanctions include monetary penalties, fee awards, adverse rulings, and public reprimands (Consequences of Inadequate Legal Research).
